title: Beyond the Gallery Talk: How The Met Invites Artists to Think Out Loud
content:
What happens when you ask an artist not to explain a work of art, but to have a conversation with it?

At the Creative Museums Summit 2026, Isaac Poole, Associate Educator in Public Programs at The Metropolitan Museum of Art shared an exciting programme that set out to explore this question.

Most museum talks are built on interpretation: an expert stands before an object and tells us what it means. The Met’s Explorations series turns that around. Artists, playwrights, designers and choreographers are invited into direct dialogue with objects in the collection, responding through the methods of their own discipline. The focus is on their personal relationship with a work, not commentary about it.

The results have ranged from an audio guide that becomes a meditation, to a dance performed before a Tiffany window, to a comedy in which a marble muse talks back. Together they offer a model for reaching adult audiences that any museum can learn from.
snippet: What happens when you ask an artist not to explain a work of art, but to have a conversation with it?
creator: Manuel Charr

title: How National Museums Liverpool Built an Adult Craft Programme That Pays Its Way
content:
Faced with flat budgets and a new target to generate income, National Museums Liverpool’s Learning and Participation team launched a £20 hands-on craft series for adults. Two years on, Meet and Make is paying its way, funding free community sessions and helping strangers become friends. Participation facilitator Faye Richardson-Hignett shared how it works at the Creative Museums Summit.

Most adults stop making art somewhere around the end of school. Somewhere along the way, many decide they are “not creative” and quietly opt out.

Meet and Make was designed to undo that. Each month, National Museums Liverpool (NML) runs a two-hour workshop where adults try a craft, perhaps for the first time in years. The brief to participants is simple: drop any expectation that the result has to be good, have a go, then head to the café for a brew and a chat.

“The whole aim of this is to make it really, really simple, really, really easy,” Richardson-Hignett told the Summit. Her hope is that other museums will see how achievable it is and try something similar.

title: How English Heritage Used Poetry to Engage Young People: Lessons for Museums
content:
Museum and heritage learning teams share a common challenge: how do you help young people make a personal connection with collections and historic places, rather than simply visiting them?

English Heritage tested one answer through Inspiring Voices, inviting young people aged 11 to 25 to respond to its sites through poetry, in written, spoken, filmed and visual forms. At a MuseumNext presentation, Laura Taylor, Digital Learning Manager at English Heritage, and Domi Blackmore, Learning and Participation Programmes Manager at English Heritage, shared how the work was designed and delivered, and what they learned.

According to the speakers, eight on-site workshops reached 119 young people against a target of 50, and an online poetry festival received 168 submissions against a target of 50. These figures measure participation and reach. The team also gathered immediate before-and-after feedback, but the presentation did not report longer-term measures of connection or wellbeing.

What museum teams can learn

  • Frame it as a creative response, not “poetry”. The word can deter bookings; a broader framing widened interest.
snippet: Museum and heritage learning teams share a common challenge: how do you help young people make a personal connection with collections and historic places, rather than simply visiting them?
creator: Manuel Charr

title: The Giant Scarf Project: How Creative Making Builds Community Engagement in Museums
content:
What happens when a football museum asks a city to knit? For the National Football Museum, the answer was a scarf more than 200 metres long, made from over 1,000 segments – and a way back into a community it had become distant from.

The Giant Scarf Project ran for two years in Preston, in partnership with Preston North End Community and Education Trust. It invited football lovers and loathers, experienced knitters and complete beginners to contribute a piece of a giant bar scarf. It was designed to reach people who might not see themselves reflected in a football museum, and to reconnect the museum with the city it left in 2012.

This case study sets out how the project was delivered, what it achieved, where the team had to adapt, and four lessons for museums planning community participation projects.

The National Football Museum opened in 2001 at Deepdale, home of Preston North End. Financial pressures led it to move to Manchester in 2012, but its Research and Archive Centre has remained at Deepdale ever since.

title: How to Turn an Archive into a Community Movement: Crowdsourcing Lessons from National Library of Wales
content:
Starting in autumn 2023, around 400 volunteers transcribed the names and addresses on the 390,296 signatures of the Welsh Women’s Peace Petition of 1923–24. Most of the work was done in about 15 months.

Their effort turned a document forgotten for nearly a century into a searchable record. That record then became the starting point for a nationwide movement of discovery, creativity and connection.

Dafydd Tudur, Head of Engagement at the National Library of Wales, felt that connection first-hand. Searching the newly digitised petition, he found his great-grandmother, Selina Edwards. She had signed in the hope that her newborn daughter, Gwenllian, might grow up in a world without war.

Volunteers uncovered other voices too. Jane Florence White, a mother from Cardiff, wrote a few words beside her name to explain why she signed: “One son killed, one lost his leg, one in lunatic asylum.” Another signatory wrote simply: “No more war.” Those notes had probably gone unread since the 1920s.

title: How the Philadelphia Museum of Art Brought 600 Teen Voices Into Its American Art Galleries
content:
How do you make a major gallery reinstallation feel relevant to young people who may never have visited your museum? The Philadelphia Museum of Art answered that question with a simple tool: a postcard. Its teen programs team distributed more than 2,000 blank postcards to local teens and collected over 600 drawings back for display in the museum.

The drawings were prompted by two short instructional videos, each led by a Philadelphia teaching artist and rooted in themes from the museum’s reinstalled American art galleries. The result was a teen community engagement project that combined real curatorial depth with wide community reach, and brought new families through the museum’s doors.

The museum reinstalled its American art galleries to mark the semiquincentennial, the 250th anniversary of the United States. The new presentation, A Nation of Artists, asks a pointed question: who gets to be an American artist?

title: What the Saint Louis Art Museum Learned from Four Bold Audience Experiments
content:
What happens when a museum invites babies, dogs and stand-up comedians through its doors? At the Saint Louis Art Museum (SLAM), it became a two-year testing ground for museum audience development. Educators Jessica M. Kennedy, Erica Richard and MaryClaire Pavlick shared four of these experiments at MuseumNext: what they tried, what worked, what didn’t and what they learned along the way.

SLAM was founded in 1879 and now holds more than 38,000 works spanning five millennia and six continents. Its home, the Palace of Fine Arts, displayed 11,000 works during the 1904 World’s Fair. For more than 115 years the museum has offered free admission, and “Dedicated to Art and Free to All” is carved above its main entrance.

The museum serves a region of nearly three million people across Missouri and Illinois. Most visitors come from the City of St. Louis and St. Louis County, whose tax support makes free admission possible.

Yet free entry alone does not make everyone feel welcome. That gap is what led SLAM to the Access for All grant.
